title: Double-digit price declines in property cat reinsurance likely to persist, says JP Morgan - Reinsurance News
content:
JP Morgan, the US-based global investment bank and financial services company, expects double-digit price declines in property catastrophe reinsurance to persist into 2027, as strong industry profitability, relatively low natural catastrophe losses and an influx of capital continue to put pressure on rates. The reinsurance market, and notably property and property cat lines, have been experiencing softer pricing conditions for some time, but 2026 marked an acceleration in the pace of reductions. Following a period of exceptionally high rates in 2023 and 2024 after the so-called reset, pricing has moved progressively lower, with more substantial decreases recorded across the latest renewal periods. JP Morgan cited figures from reinsurance broker Marsh Re, formerly known as Guy Carpenter, showing that average reinsurance prices declined by approximately 12% at the January 2026 renewals. The downward trend continued into the mid-year renewal period, with global property catastrophe rates falling by 16% at the July 2026 renewals. The investment bank anticipates additional pricing pressure at the January 2027 renewals, particularly within property catastrophe lines, where it expects double-digit decreases to continue. JP Morgan attributed this outlook to several factors, including the sector’s sustained strong returns on equity (ROE), relatively benign catastrophe experience during 2026 to date and the availability of new sources of capital. JP Morgan noted that reinsurers have recorded particularly favourable financial results since 2023, with average ROEs remaining in the high teens. The bank compared this performance with the period following Hurricane Katrina, when increased property catastrophe rates and elevated interest rates supported similarly strong industry returns. However, the investment bank cautioned that extended periods of consistently high profitability have been relatively uncommon in the reinsurance industry. Historically, fluctuations in catastrophe losses have contributed to greater volatility in earnings than has been observed in recent years, suggesting that the current level of profitability may become harder to sustain. JP Morgan also indicated that the financial consequences of declining reinsurance rates are beginning to emerge, particularly in underwriting performance, despite the sector’s continued resilience in the near term. The bank pointed to Munich Re as one of the first major reinsurers to demonstrate the effects of weaker pricing on its combined ratio expectations during 2026. At the beginning of the year, Munich Re’s normalised combined ratio was expected to stand at 80%, but this had deteriorated to approximately 82% by the second quarter. While other reinsurers have so far experienced a more limited impact, JP Morgan believes the broader industry will find it increasingly difficult to offset continued rate reductions. The bank therefore expects underwriting margins to face growing pressure over the next two years as lower pricing gradually affects financial performance. title: The blue wave is changing the AI trade - J.P. Morgan Private Bank

The U.S. economy and the stock market have proven resilient in 2026, even in the face of higher interest rates, geopolitical volatility and yet another energy shock. Whereas the U.S. consumer, aided by fiscal stimulus and tax cuts, is still spending, a growing driver of GDP growth remains the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out. In the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, the Democratic party gained control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, setting the stage for gridlock with a Republican president—especially when it comes to the continued development and adoption of AI across the country. Investors feared a federal moratorium that mirrors some of the state-led initiatives to curb the build-out, in response to affordability and zoning concerns. So, it’s only natural that the outcome of the elections initially sent stock market futures plunging nearly 2% before rebounding with significant volatility in technology companies even days after the result. Democratic gains increase the likelihood of tougher scrutiny around data center development, electricity affordability and who pays for new grid infrastructure. This can create near-term uncertainty for sectors that trade in line with AI developments like utilities—especially those with exposure to fast-growing markets like Texas and Georgia that offer affordable land, labor and both energy and water access. Even as investors reprice that risk, the structural backdrop remains in place. Hyperscaler investment is expected to continue. Electrification and the grid build-out are still pressing needs in order to support higher power demand and capital spending. Stopping the data center build-out is still a tall order. Initial efforts to curb the data center build-out began over the summer. Any new policies to slow or restrict new connections would build on a process that’s already underway. More notable policy changes could be around who bears the costs of additional grid connections, changes to tax exemptions, stricter financial commitments and emergency curtailment requirements, among others. While much of this uncertainty was priced in leading into the elections, the magnitude of the Democratic gains was not. And that’s changing the nature of the tech trade underneath the hood. In an environment where regulation could change even if the most AI-friendly states, companies with existing compute and data center projects—like the hyperscalers—have the edge. Plus, additional regulatory proposals target new developments, not existing ones, which could strengthen the position of companies with operational data centers, secured power and established customers. Combined with any potential moderation in AI growth and the ability to meet greater construction and permitting standards, the established lead that some of the biggest tech companies have is even more beneficial relative to the parts of the tech trade that rely on the incremental build-out. And that’s something investors are already pricing, sending the message that owning productive capacity today is different from depending on its construction tomorrow—even if that means factoring in potential regulatory risk. Before the policy details have even been settled, or formally proposed, investors have already repriced these possibilities. It’s most visible in parts of the “picks and shovels” AI infrastructure trade—the part of the market that rallied on the certainty of the build-out even as the return on investment faced remain in question. The 24-month forward price-to-earnings ratio of the MVIS US Listed Semiconductor Index has halved since June. After trading at a peak of 22.5 times forward earnings in June, the index currently trades at 11.4 times forward earnings. That’s at a valuation lower than when investors were digesting the beginning of the conflict in Iran, Liberation Day and the stock market lows of 2022. It reflects a market questioning the durability of the industry’s earnings and continued growth in capital expenditures. But that’s where the opportunity may lie. Yes, regulation is subject to change, but the scale of economic growth that has come from this sector alone may bear some impact on the level and willingness to limit continued development. The AI trade is far from over, but it is evolving. Financing, regulatory and power constraints can mean a bumpy road ahead, but unless end demand falters, the risk of an inventory overhang and earnings slowdown may already be baked into valuations. As the structural backdrop of the AI build-out remains in place, the key is to determine which companies have the lead in an undeniable technological evolution that can broaden out in the years to come. The U.S. economy and the stock market have proven resilient in 2026, even in the face of higher interest rates, geopolitical volatility and yet another energy shock. Whereas the U.S. consumer, aided by fiscal stimulus and tax cuts, is still spending, a growing driver of GDP growth remains the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out. In the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, the Democratic party gained control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, setting the stage for gridlock with a Republican president—especially when it comes to the continued development and adoption of AI across the country. Investors feared a federal moratorium that mirrors some of the state-led initiatives to curb the build-out, in response to affordability and zoning concerns. So, it’s only natural that the outcome of the elections initially sent stock market futures plunging nearly 2% before rebounding with significant volatility in technology companies even days after the result. Democratic gains increase the likelihood of tougher scrutiny around data center development, electricity affordability and who pays for new grid infrastructure. This can create near-term uncertainty for sectors that trade in line with AI developments like utilities—especially those with exposure to fast-growing markets like Texas and Georgia that offer affordable land, labor and both energy and water access. Even as investors reprice that risk, the structural backdrop remains in place. Hyperscaler investment is expected to continue. Electrification and the grid build-out are still pressing needs in order to support higher power demand and capital spending. Stopping the data center build-out is still a tall order. Initial efforts to curb the data center build-out began over the summer. Any new policies to slow or restrict new connections would build on a process that’s already underway. More notable policy changes could be around who bears the costs of additional grid connections, changes to tax exemptions, stricter financial commitments and emergency curtailment requirements, among others. While much of this uncertainty was priced in leading into the elections, the magnitude of the Democratic gains was not. And that’s changing the nature of the tech trade underneath the hood. In an environment where regulation could change even if the most AI-friendly states, companies with existing compute and data center projects—like the hyperscalers—have the edge. Plus, additional regulatory proposals target new developments, not existing ones, which could strengthen the position of companies with operational data centers, secured power and established customers. Combined with any potential moderation in AI growth and the ability to meet greater construction and permitting standards, the established lead that some of the biggest tech companies have is even more beneficial relative to the parts of the tech trade that rely on the incremental build-out. And that’s something investors are already pricing, sending the message that owning productive capacity today is different from depending on its construction tomorrow—even if that means factoring in potential regulatory risk. Before the policy details have even been settled, or formally proposed, investors have already repriced these possibilities. It’s most visible in parts of the “picks and shovels” AI infrastructure trade—the part of the market that rallied on the certainty of the build-out even as the return on investment faced remain in question. The 24-month forward price-to-earnings ratio of the MVIS US Listed Semiconductor Index has halved since June. After trading at a peak of 22.5 times forward earnings in June, the index currently trades at 11.4 times forward earnings. That’s at a valuation lower than when investors were digesting the beginning of the conflict in Iran, Liberation Day and the stock market lows of 2022. It reflects a market questioning the durability of the industry’s earnings and continued growth in capital expenditures. But that’s where the opportunity may lie. Yes, regulation is subject to change, but the scale of economic growth that has come from this sector alone may bear some impact on the level and willingness to limit continued development. The AI trade is far from over, but it is evolving. Financing, regulatory and power constraints can mean a bumpy road ahead, but unless end demand falters, the risk of an inventory overhang and earnings slowdown may already be baked into valuations. As the structural backdrop of the AI build-out remains in place, the key is to determine which companies have the lead in an undeniable technological evolution that can broaden out in the years to come. Energy markets and term premiums are connected in a way they haven’t been before. Executive Director, Global Investment Strategist, J.P. Morgan Private Bank The upward march in bond yields continues to drive the market narrative, but the logic has shifted. The move began in the early summer with a Federal Reserve (Fed) that investors initially perceived as hawkish, but a series of softer jobs and inflation reports has cast it in a different light. Now, the drivers look a little different: They’re a combination of worries around global fiscal deficits, an increase in hyperscaler issuance and a rise in refined product prices. And that’s on top of U.S. economic growth. Since the July meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), by far the greatest driver of higher yields has been an increase in term premium – the extra compensation investors demand to hold longer-dated government debt amid elevated uncertainty. Second to that, it’s robust economic activity. Notably, and in contrast to most media narratives, upward pressure from explicitly more hawkish monetary policy hasn’t been a factor. On the surface, rangebound oil prices six months into the conflict in Iran haven’t spooked markets in the same way they did in March. Even with escalation in the Middle East conflict, Brent crude has traded within a range of $80 to $100 per barrel, to which both financial markets and the economy have adapted. Instead, the pressure is building underneath the hood – in the refined products space. Whereas oil and gasoline prices have risen 32% and 37%, respectively, since the conflict began, diesel and jet fuel have risen by much more – by 50% and 60%, respectively. The problem is that the United States, although oil-rich and currently the largest producer and exporter of oil in the world, primarily has light crude. American refineries, largely built to convert heavy crude into those refined products, are nearing their maximum capacity. So even though light crude is readily available, it doesn’t necessarily alleviate the rising prices of those refined products, or the potential readthrough into more consumer-facing products like airfares. The relationship has created a synergy between refining margins and bond yields. As investors measure the impact of the conflict, the building relationship shows pressure in that part of the commodities market is starting to align with the move in bond yields. Higher energy prices across products are not necessarily signaling an imminent downturn. Instead, they’re reinforcing a market environment where growth remains firm enough to support consumer resilience and spending. That’s partially why term premiums have continued to rise. For equity investors, the key risk is not necessarily higher oil prices but higher discount rates that materialize quickly rather than gradually – especially as autumn approaches and the stock market faces what has historically been stocks’ weakest month of the year. Seasonality is often dismissed as market folklore, but many calendar effects are rooted in predictable flows. Tax deadlines, pension contributions, portfolio rebalancing, corporate buybacks and options expiries all occur on known schedules, creating recurring shifts in liquidity and investor positioning. These dynamics rarely drive markets on their own, but they can amplify existing trends – like the effect of a move in bond yields – and tend to set the final quarter of the year up for gains. The recent rise in bond yields is a reminder that not all inflation risks originate with monetary policy. title: JPMorgan Chase & Co. Warns a Rapid Rate Rise Could Shake the Financial System - TradingView
content: JPMorgan Chase & Co. JPM is preparing for interest rates to move in either direction, but a rapid rise poses a broader risk to the financial system, according to Charles Bristow, the bank’s head of treasury and chief investment officer. Bristow said the bank has stress-tested its balance sheet against higher rates and does not have a single “nightmare scenario.” His greater concern is that a sudden repricing could leave other institutions unable to adjust their balance sheets quickly, undermine confidence and trigger competition for funding. “If the move to higher rates needs to be too fast, it will have very non-linear and unpredictable outcomes,” he said. Bristow said the market was pricing just over two interest-rate hikes through the end of 2027, near what he considers the lower end of a credible range. While he said market pricing was not far off on a probability-weighted basis, he remained cautious about the risk of rates moving higher. For JPMorgan’s investment portfolio, he said the more consequential question is where the market settles on the economy’s tendency toward inflation and the Federal Reserve’s neutral rate. Medium-term rate forwards have risen to around 5% from 3% about four years ago, he said, reflecting a shift toward an environment of higher growth, investment and inflation pressure. The bank’s approach to managing the duration of its balance sheet has not fundamentally changed, Bristow said. JPMorgan has generally avoided longer-dated investments because it believed markets had underpriced a return to a period of substantial public- and private-sector infrastructure investment. He added that current pricing makes that position harder to maintain than it was four years ago. He also said a proposed accounting change allowing hedging of held-to-maturity securities could give the bank room, at the margin, to take more interest-rate exposure in low-credit-risk instruments within that portfolio. Asked about a decline in third-quarter share repurchases, Bristow said the bank’s sustainable dividend is its primary capital-return commitment. Beyond that, JPMorgan weighs buybacks against potential uses of capital over the medium term. He said growth in risk-weighted assets was running at approximately a double-digit compound annual rate and that the bank was already finding organic opportunities to deploy capital. Retaining capital for future opportunities was prudent, he said, given the bank’s cost of capital and demand for financing. On deposits, Bristow said customers have had considerable time to seek higher rates since the 2022–2023 cycle. He said JPMorgan’s balances are behaving as expected for a bank focused on operating deposits, including retail checking accounts and balances associated with payments and custody services. The bank is nevertheless stress-testing outcomes in which policy rates move beyond their recent range. Bristow welcomed greater transparency and averaging in bank stress testing, saying a more predictable process could reduce the capital buffer banks hold against volatility. He also supported aspects of proposed changes to capital requirements for globally systemically important banks, including smoothing and smaller surcharge buckets, but said regulators should recalibrate coefficients more fully and explain a proposed change involving short-term wholesale funding. Some proposed rules could make low-risk intermediation businesses unable to meet return hurdles, he said. JPMorgan would continue serving clients across business lines, he added, though the rules could discourage investment in such activity at the margin. Bristow said he saw no signs of market stress, but that liquidity was a binding constraint for the banking system. He pointed to a relationship between marginal lending and bank borrowing as evidence that lending is increasingly being funded through borrowing rather than excess cash. JPMorgan has about $1.3 trillion in liquid assets, he said, while noting that other high-quality assets receive no liquidity value under current treatment. He argued that the distinction can curtail systemwide liquidity capacity. A smaller Federal Reserve balance sheet would withdraw liquidity from a system already operating at a constraint, Bristow said. If policymakers pursue that path, he said, they should consider liquidity reforms alongside it to avoid liquidity cliffs or higher borrowing costs. Asked whether AI agents could make deposits move more quickly between institutions, Bristow said banks need to monitor potential structural changes over the coming years. He expects adoption to be gradual and does not see it fundamentally changing the checking-account business model. Still, he said, faster-moving and more rate-sensitive deposits could reduce banks’ demand for longer-duration assets and affect credit availability. Meanwhile, Firedancer opened a bug bounty that pays triple for Alpenglow findings. Developers also gained web3.js v3, a monitoring tool, and a plan to retire durable nonces. Institutions kept building settlement tools alongside the protocol work. The Solana Foundation released Solana DvP with input from J.P. Morgan on October 6. Two weeks later, J.P. Morgan Asset Management brought its MONY and JLTXX funds to Solana. Securitize, Mirae Asset Securities, and Ondo each added products as well. Hong Kong produced the month’s regional cluster, led by Anchorpoint’s plan to issue HKDAP natively on Solana. Alpenglow went live on mainnet on October 21 in epoch 1064. It replaced TowerBFT, the consensus protocol Solana has run since launch. Solana Compass places the handoff at slot 459,653,000. Solana’s upgrade page sets a finality target of roughly 150 milliseconds, down from about 12.8 seconds. However, no independent party has published post-activation finality measurements yet. Before mainnet, a test cluster finalized 96% of blocks on the fast path at 214 milliseconds. This first phase ships Votor, the new voting protocol, inside Agave 4.3. Execution stays the same, so programs, transactions, and fees work exactly as before. Vote transactions no longer appear in blocks, and “confirmed” and “finalized” now describe the same state. Validators needed an Agave-based client at version 4.3.2 and at least 0.8 SOL in their vote account. That balance covers the Validator Admission Ticket fee. Firedancer then joined the new consensus and began removing its TowerBFT code. The path to launch carried some risk. On October 19, an Alpenglow tracker flagged 45% of stake as not ready. Most of it ran older 4.3 releases. Anza had already named version 4.3.2 the recommended release on October 16. After activation, Marinade tied some skipped leader slots to Alpenglow, and Agave 4.4.0-rc.1 carries a fix. Phase two, Rotor, will replace Turbine for block propagation, but Anza has not scheduled it. Anza CEO Brennan Watt explained the launch decisions in an interview with Genfinity days later. The final step of SIMD-0525 went live on October 9 at epoch 1053. It cut slot times from 250 milliseconds to 200. Earlier steps landed on August 21, August 28, and September 18. The first full epoch at the new target averaged 218.3 milliseconds and lasted 26.2 hours. Blockhashes now expire after 30 seconds, and each leader window runs 800 milliseconds. Follow-on proposals came quickly. On October 10, Watt proposed raising the block compute limit from 50 million back to 100 million compute units. Agave also raised its default snapshot interval to 200,000 slots. Later, Agave 4.4.0 delivered what Anza called Solana’s final rent cuts. Anza asked for 20% of stake on the release candidate by October 30. It then told validators to upgrade to 4.4.0 three days early. Firedancer launched its bug bounty program on October 16 at bounty.firedancer.io. Through November 20, the program doubles rewards for all valid reports. It also triples rewards for findings related to Alpenglow. Each submission burns 1 SOL to discourage spam. The program follows Jump’s $1 million Immunefi audit contest from April and May. That contest drew 809 reports and 127 unique findings, and the most severe rated High. Firedancer also shipped four mainnet releases during October. The Firedancer bug bounty platform is live at https://t.co/SxvcrvKOM8! Now thru Nov 20th: 2x rewards across the board; 3x for Alpenglow.

We’re sharing our experience running a $1,000,000 bounty contest: how Firedancer’s security model works, notable bugs researchers found, what we learned, and some lessons about triaging AI-assisted reports at scale.

Read it here. https://t.co/Z5ivnggknD The October changelogs added several tools for builders. web3.js v3 became ready for general use, and version 3.1 followed on October 16. It rebuilds the classic JavaScript API on Kit and adds a new wallet adapter. On October 6, Solana published a durable nonce deprecation plan. Removal will come about six months after a replacement goes live on mainnet. Candidates include Anza’s Programmatic Signer and Blueshift’s Vector. Research and monitoring work landed too. A geo-aware leader schedule study for SIMD-0675 proposes reordering leaders to cut handoff latency. Notably, every validator keeps the same number of leader windows. Solana Microscope offers open-source program monitoring with Grafana dashboards and alerts through Slack, Telegram, and PagerDuty. Additionally, a Squads builder tested Falcon-512 post-quantum multisig voting on mainnet. On October 30, Watt proposed replacing standalone SIMDs with a single Solana Protocol Specification. The Solana Foundation launched Solana DvP on October 6. It is an open-source escrow program for delivery-versus-payment settlement under the MIT license. Both legs of a trade settle in one atomic transaction, or neither settles. J.P. Morgan contributed input on institutional settlement practice, though the release does not describe the bank as a user. The program supports SPL Token and Token-2022, including permanent delegates, pausable tokens, and transfer hooks. Any bank, custodian, or exchange can serve as the settlement agent. An external audit cleared the code, and the Foundation calls it ready for real funds. Privacy features remain on the roadmap, and the Foundation wants design partners before a production release. Catherine Gu leads digital asset products at the Foundation. “Atomic settlement removes counterparty risk that is inherent in traditional finance,” she said. Rhodel D’souza of J.P. Morgan said the bank was “pleased to contribute our settlement expertise.” Our launch coverage walks through the escrow flow. The code sits on GitHub. J.P. Morgan Asset Management expanded its tokenized money market funds to Solana on October 22. Qualified U.S. investors can now access MONY and JLTXX on Solana through Morgan Money. MONY first launched on Ethereum. The announcement landed one day after Alpenglow went live. As a result, J.P. Morgan appeared twice in Solana’s October news, once as an adviser and once as an issuer. The Genfinity breakdown covers the fund details. Mirae Asset Securities’ Hong Kong unit issued tokenized funding notes on Solana on October 28. The notes are USD six-month floating rate notes under its US$3 billion Guaranteed Structured Note Programme. That $3 billion figure describes the program, and Mirae did not disclose the issue size. Singapore-regulated Marketnode acted as authorized distributor. Mirae offered the notes only through private placement to institutions. It also ran issuance, payments, and lifecycle management on its own infrastructure, with support from the Solana Foundation. Ondo launched Intelligent Portfolios on Solana on October 29 for eligible non-U.S. investors. Each of the seven portfolios packs tokenized stocks and ETFs into a single token, and smart contracts handle rebalancing. Three portfolios follow BlackRock model allocations for high income, high growth, and diversified growth. However, BlackRock does not sponsor, manage, or distribute them. Ondo designed the other four in-house. Earlier, on October 19, LI.FI brought Ondo’s tokenized stocks and ETFs to Solana through LI.FI Intents. Ondo Intelligent Portfolios are now live on Solana, including three portfolios powered by BlackRock.

Seven curated portfolios spanning income, growth, and thematic exposure, each delivered as a single onchain transferable token:

→ BRAINon: AI Leaders
→ YLD5on: 5% Targeted Income
→ YLD8on: 8% Targeted Income
→ MAG7Xon: Magnificent 7 & Crypto
→ BLKHIon: Ondo High Income Powered by BlackRock
→ BLKGRWon: Ondo High Growth Powered by BlackRock
→ BLKDIGon: Ondo Diversified Growth Powered by BlackRock

Each portfolio combines assets in one onchain token, with transparent holdings and programmatic rebalancing.

Ondo Intelligent Portfolios are going live on Solana with several launch partner wallets and apps, including Titan, 1inch, LI․FI, Jumper, and more.

This is just the beginning of a broader move onchain, as Ondo expands access to institutional asset allocation expertise across the Solana ecosystem. The Solana Foundation’s asset directory added the Solana Asset Registry on October 29. It lists 3,293 tokenized assets across fiat-backed, crypto-backed, fixed income, equity, and private fund categories. The registry shows data from Allium, RWA.xyz, and CoinGecko side by side, and it offers an API. At launch, it valued USDC on Solana at $6.53 billion through Allium and $6.50 billion through RWA.xyz. Other institutional items rounded out the month. Fidelity’s FCAT published a report on October 17 that found Solana more reliable than in prior years. The same report noted that stake, hosting, and client software remain concentrated. Meanwhile, Google previewed MPC custody for banks, with Solana support “coming soon.” PrimeRevenue said it will tokenize electronic time drafts on Solana, without a launch date. Securitize launched Securitize Stocks on Solana on October 8 with 12 U.S. equities. The lineup includes Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Tesla, and Palantir. A share backs each token 1:1, and holders own a security entitlement through Securitize Markets. Securitize calls this structure a convertible entitlement token. Trades settle in USDC, and Jump Trading makes markets on Securitize’s Solana PropAMM. Additionally, RQD handles clearing, custody, and settlement. EU investors can access the stocks through Securitize Europe. Ripple Prime said it plans to support the tokens, though no live integration exists yet. Following today’s launch of Securitize Stocks on @solana, our CEO @carlosdomingo joined @CNBC to discuss bringing stocks onchain in the U.S. and the path toward 24/7 trading.

Tokenize the World. https://t.co/UKOPMtdBoH Kamino opened a Backpack market on October 28. Users can now borrow USDC against tokenized SpaceX, Micron, SK Hynix, and SanDisk shares from Backpack Securities. The market gives tokenized equities a credit use beyond trading. Earlier, on October 16, Spout raised $2 million for 0% interest loans on tokenized U.S. stocks. It funds those loans through covered calls. Introducing the Backpack Market on Kamino.

Kamino is expanding loans backed by tokenized equity on Solana with @Backpack Securities, bringing 1:1-backed, redeemable tokenized U.S.-listed equities directly into onchain credit markets. https://t.co/yKRDP3SYoE Backpack Securities and Sunrise added listings throughout the month. Tokenized BlackRock stock arrived on October 2 and trades around the clock on Raydium. Powerus shares listed a day after its merger closed. Later weeks brought the EWZ Brazil ETF, Ferrari, and Broadcom. Sunrise also carried assets from other networks onto Solana, including NEAR and Zcash. Raydium’s Q3 net revenue rose 264% to $7.99 million, which Blockworks tied to tokenized stocks and LaunchLab. Samsung Wallet selected Solana for cross-border USDC transfers on October 7. U.S. users can send USDC starting in the last week of October. The feature covers 82 million U.S. Galaxy devices at launch, and more markets will follow. It includes fiat on-ramps and off-ramps, with Coinbase and Bastion handling custody and payments. Solana Compass reports that Sui also serves as a network partner. We found no post-launch confirmation that the feature went live by month’s end. Solana Foundation President Lily Liu framed the deal as a turning point. “We’re seeing the moment when stablecoins stop being a crypto product and start being how people move money,” she said. Woncheol Chai of Samsung Electronics said “Solana helps us bring that experience to Samsung’s scale.” The Foundation’s post also cites more than $5.25 trillion in Solana stablecoin volume during 2026. Our launch coverage details the rollout. Polygon’s Open Money Stack added Solana on October 29. Through one API, it links U.S. bank pay-ins to USDC, USDT, or PYUSD on Solana. It then routes funds back out to banks, cards, or cash. Polygon warned that support does not guarantee availability for every bank, token, or jurisdiction. Earlier, on October 6, Circle’s USDC bridge added Solana and linked it to 18 other chains. On October 24, Circle Gateway brought unified EURC balances to Solana. Business payments gained ground as well. Ramp added USDG on Solana on October 16 with zero-fee dollar conversions. Meanwhile, Western Union widened distribution for USDPT, its Solana stablecoin from May. Bitso listed USDPT in Mexico on October 14. A week later, Western Union tapped Noah to pay remittances into Stablecard as USDPT. At Money20/20, an X9.150 demo let one invoice settle over FedNow, RTP, or USDC on Solana. Solana is now live on @0xPolygon’s Open Money Stack.

Bank rails, wallets and conversion, connected to Solana through one integration. Businesses build where their customers already are. Anchorpoint plans to mint and redeem HKDAP natively on Solana, it said on October 30. Standard Chartered leads the joint venture, which holds one of Hong Kong’s first two HKMA stablecoin licenses. HSBC Hong Kong holds the other. HKDAP launched on Ethereum on August 12, backed 1:1 by Hong Kong dollar reserves. The Solana Foundation will also join Anchorpoint’s Tokenised Money Adoption Programme alongside PwC Hong Kong. However, Anchorpoint gave no Solana start date, and its FAQ still listed only Ethereum. Until Anchorpoint publishes a Solana mint address, no Solana token calling itself HKDAP is the licensed stablecoin. BREAKING: Anchorpoint brings HKDAP, the Hong Kong dollar stablecoin, to Solana.

In its first collaboration with a public network, HKDAP will mint and redeem natively on Solana, settling near-instantly and reaching everything from retail payments to tokenized assets. https://t.co/sq7zMB9UdW The Hong Kong government named Solana Company a strategic enterprise on October 22. The Nasdaq-listed firm joined 17 others in the seventh OASES batch. It calls itself the only blockchain infrastructure company OASES onboarded in 2026. Solana Company opened a Hong Kong office as its Asia-Pacific headquarters. It also plans to run Solana validators in the city under its Pacific Backbone initiative. The release disclosed no investment figure, subsidy, or start date. 🚨JUST IN: @Solana treasury firm @Solana_Company ($HSDT) has been selected by Hong Kong’s government as a strategic enterprise.

The company has opened an office in Hong Kong to serve as its Asia-Pacific headquarters and plans to operate Solana validators in the city. https://t.co/o6385KMjNP The Pando Solana ETF began trading in Hong Kong on October 13 under ticker 2831. Together with the Mirae notes, it gave Hong Kong four Solana stories in one month. One setback balanced the list. Organizers postponed Solana Accelerate Shanghai on October 16, the day it was set to open. They cited venue logistics, while Lily Liu pointed to the registration cap. No new date has surfaced. The Solana Policy Institute filed a comment letter on October 22. It responds to the SEC’s September 17 innovation exemption for tokenized securities venues. That order requires venues to run on a “public, permissionless distributed ledger” but leaves the term undefined. CEO Miller Whitehouse-Levine and General Counsel Patrick Wilson signed the letter. They asked the SEC to judge permissionlessness by who controls transaction ordering and the validator set. Their five factors draw on the Senate CLARITY Act discussion draft. The letter also requests a narrow carve-out for temporary emergency measures, such as pauses or patches. Operators would disclose each one and file a post-incident report. The carve-out “would preserve an operator’s ability to protect investors without permitting ongoing centralized control,” the letter states. Other filers took different positions on the same docket. Hedera argued on October 9 that public permissioned networks should qualify, and SIFMA asked for clarity on October 19. The SEC has not responded publicly. Broader rulemaking continued during the month. On October 5, the CFTC issued an advance notice on retail crypto transactions. The Federal Register published the related market rules on October 13. Then, on October 21, SEC staff released an FAQ on the innovation exemption. Venues must now publish their operating and access standards at least 30 days before launch. None of these actions targets Solana specifically, but together they shape where tokenized stock venues can operate. U.S. spot Solana ETFs recorded about $99.6 million in net outflows through October 27, according to SoSoValue data. That day alone saw $19.16 million leave, the largest daily outflow since December 2025. Outflows hit all five sessions in the week of October 5. Total net assets ended the month near $1.5 billion, down from $1.93 billion in September. However, outflows explain only part of that drop. On a brighter note, VanEck’s VSOL declared its first staking distribution of $964,960 on October 7. Treasury companies moved in opposite directions. Forward Industries ended its fiscal fourth quarter with 8.5 million SOL after adding 948,601 SOL. DeFi Development Corp passed 2.6 million SOL on October 30. In contrast, SkyAI, formerly Sharps Technology, sold its last SOL on October 15. It held more than 2 million SOL in mid-September. SkyAI then ran a tender offer of up to $201.3 million and rejected a Forward Industries proposal. Holder Bastion Trading refused to tender and demanded sale details, and the parties settled on October 28. For decades, market access has come down to whose servers sit closest to the matching engine.

@KyleSamani, Chairman of Forward Industries, on what changes when the engine is everywhere.

The future of finance runs on @solana. https://t.co/WGKJBBSJyp Attackers began draining Binance at 20:05 UTC on October 29. TRM Labs estimates the theft at roughly $6.36 billion and attributes it to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Within minutes, 970,500 SOL left Binance’s Solana hot wallet. Kamino paused borrowing in its SOL/BTC market at 22:03 UTC as a precaution. Co-founder Marius Ciubotariu said Kamino blocked the attacker’s wallet within five minutes of spotting it. Borrowing resumed the next afternoon, about 17 hours later, while deposits and repayments ran normally throughout. Jupiter Lend faced a different problem. It had no Binance exposure, but a liquidity crunch queued its withdrawals. At one point, its USDC vault had about 7,900 USDC withdrawable against 420 million supplied. USDC withdrawals returned about 13 hours later. Velocity also paused new deposits on October 31 to keep stolen funds out. No Solana protocol reported losses, and attackers exploited no Solana code. Solana Mobile named Ledger its first hardware expansion partner on October 15. The companies announced it on stage at Ledger Op3n in Paris. Ledger Atom, a touchscreen Android device, will ship with the Seeker app and dApp Store. It targets summer 2027. Additionally, Solana Mobile released Seeker Connect on October 21, a one-tap wallet SDK for Expo, Kotlin, and web apps. A buy-and-burn for the SKR token also started on October 15. Jupiter and BitGo launched an institutional validator on October 28. BitGo clients can now stake SOL directly from custody. Jupiter also opened a Bridge beta that compares five providers. Meanwhile, Solflare launched Earn on October 26, with in-wallet USDC yield powered by Kamino. On the infrastructure side, Helius opened preconfirmations to all paid plans on October 17. Jito added direct bundle ingest for BAM, and Sanctum released swSOL, which pays staking yield to integrators. We’re excited to announce partnership with @BitGo  to launch a validator built for institutions.  

BitGo’s institutional clients can now stake SOL with Jupiter, directly from their existing custody accounts. 

Solana’s leading DeFi platform, meet the custodian institutions trust. Akash Network chose Solana to replace its Cosmos chain on October 26. Separately, Orca and Loopscale agreed to merge into a new entity called Formation on October 8. Beezie wound down its Base deployment and consolidated on Solana. Yuga Labs launched Mudwater, a physical and digital BAYC trading card game, on Solana. Additionally, the first Wakefern grocery stores went live on the Helium Network. The Foundation also published its Solana and AI thesis, which calls Solana “the democratization layer for AI.” Four Genfinity interviews in October showed why teams choose Solana. Anza CEO Brennan Watt discussed shipping Alpenglow on a live network securing over $50 billion. He said new features had to run under both consensus systems during development. He also described Rotor and geographic awareness as the next steps. Earlier, R3 CEO Richard Brown explained why R3 picked Solana for Corda protocol. He expected R3 to choose the EVM, but parallel execution and audited token standards changed his mind. On October 1, OnRe CEO Dan Roberts described moving $300 million in reinsurance premiums onchain. He argued that composability, not tokenization alone, creates the value. As a result, ONyc now supports lending markets, tranches, and fixed-yield products from one base asset. Meanwhile, Rosentica founder Natsuki walked through One Arena, a game layer for tokenized graded cards. Players battle with real Pokemon and One Piece cards, and winners take the cards home. Solana processed 5.01 billion non-vote transactions in October, up 5.9%, according to DeFi Development Corp. That marks the second-highest month on record. Daily active addresses rose 9.0% to 2.84 million. However, spot DEX volume fell to $61.0 billion from $78.3 billion in September. Bitquery also traced 22.7% of Raydium CLMM volume to one wash-trading wallet, which warrants caution on volume figures. App revenue reached about $158 million in the 30 days to October 24, up from $146 million. Stablecoin supply declined from its September record of about $17.3 billion. Late October readings ranged between $15.2 billion and $15.8 billion. Real-world asset value on Solana ran between $4.4 billion and $5.1 billion, depending on the tracker. Bitwise reported that 69% of SOL supply sat staked at the end of Q3 across 659 validators. These monthly figures come from third-party trackers rather than the Foundation, so treat them as estimates. 10 DAYS TO BREAKPOINT. title: Democrats to probe JPMorgan's relationship with Jeffrey Epstein when they take Senate control - CNBC
content:
Senate Democrats are gearing up to investigate JPMorgan Chase’s banking relationship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein once they take control of Congress early next year. Democratic staffers on the Senate Finance Committee intend to home in on how high-ranking executives at JPMorgan handled Epstein, a source familiar with the panel’s thinking told CNBC on Thursday. The person spoke on condition of anonymity because the probe of the nation’s biggest bank has not been announced. The Finance Committee is likely to be chaired beginning in January by Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat who currently is the panel’s ranking member. Wyden has made clear he plans to make full use of the subpoena powers that committee majorities wield. Democratic staffers aim to focus in particular on decisions about Epstein made by Mary Callahan Erdoes, the CEO of JPMorgan’s asset and wealth management division, the source said. JPMorgan declined to comment. The bank has previously said it regrets any association with Epstein but that it did not assist him in committing crimes. In a 2023 deposition, Erdoes said she was aware as early as 2006 that Epstein was accused of paying cash to have underage girls brought to his home. Epstein had been a client of the bank since 1998. Epstein became a registered sex offender after pleading guilty in 2008 in Florida to a state criminal charge of procuring an underage girl for prostitution. JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon in his own, later deposition in 2023, said Erdoes had authority to cut off Epstein as a client. She did not take that step until 2013. Epstein, a former friend of President Donald Trump, ex-President Bill Clinton and many other high-profile people, died in a jailhouse suicide in August 2019, weeks after being arrested on federal child sex trafficking charges. A lawyer for the U.S. Virgin Islands told a federal judge in New York in 2023 that JPMorgan “was a full-service bank for Jeffrey Epstein’s sex trafficking,” and that it waited until after he killed himself to notify the Treasury Department of $1 billion in suspicious transactions related to trafficking by Epstein. “This was a CYA [cover your a--] reporting after 16 years of all of the monies flowing in his JPMorgan accounts after he was dead,” the lawyer, Mimi Liu, said. JPMorgan has blamed former investment banking chief Jes Staley for concealing or failing to report criminal activity related to Epstein, with whom he had a close relationship. Staley, who left JPMorgan in 2013 and later became CEO of Barclays before stepping down in 2021, has denied knowledge of Epstein’s crimes. House Oversight Chair James Comer, R-Ky., after a closed-door interview with Staley in July, said that the former executive had encouraged JPMorgan to keep Epstein as a client. In mid-2023, JPMorgan agreed to a $290 million settlement with victims of Epstein without admitting wrongdoing. That same year, JPMorgan agreed to pay $75 million to settle a separate lawsuit by the U.S. Virgin Islands alleging that the bank facilitated and benefited from the sex trafficking of young women by Epstein. In August, Wyden released a report accusing top officials at multiple banks of “looking the other way” as Epstein moved hundreds of millions of dollars to finance a yearslong sex trafficking operation. “The report exposes how top bankers shielded Epstein from federal scrutiny by delaying the reporting of Epstein’s suspicious financial activity to the U.S. government, likely in violation of federal anti-money-laundering laws,” Wyden’s office said in a statement that month. “It includes new details about the extent of suspicious activity reported by Deutsche Bank after Epstein’s death, new details from bank reports filed about suspicious transfers to Epstein through accounts at Bank of America, and names top officials at JPMorgan Chase and other banks who were responsible for reporting Epstein’s shady activities to the government but instead protected Epstein in order to gain access to Leon Black and other billionaires.” Black, former CEO of Apollo Global Management, was revealed to have paid Epstein $158 million for financial advice in the years after his 2008 conviction. In September, Black sued the House oversight panel, seeking to block subpoenas it had issued him for his testimony and for documents related to its Epstein probe. On Wednesday, Black sued Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is poised to become chair of the Oversight Committee in the next Congress, alleging Garcia defamed him in statements regarding Epstein. The lawsuit focuses on Garcia’s claims in a TV interview that Black “is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes” and “was one of the last people to actually interact” with Epstein before his death, among others. The Department of Justice’s mountain of files related to Epstein became a major focus in late 2025 and early 2026, after Congress passed a bill ordering the DOJ to make those records public. Trump’s name is referenced thousands of times in the files that have been released. The president has not been charged with any wrongdoing in connection with Epstein, with whom he fell out in the early 2000s. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you. To own JPMorgan Chase, you need to be comfortable with a large, diversified bank leaning heavily on fee income, payments technology and wealth management to balance a still very credit sensitive core. The flurry of long dated callable notes mainly affects how the balance sheet is funded rather than the near term story around client activity, card volumes or payments adoption. The key short term swing factor remains how long today’s strong Markets, Investment Banking and card trends hold against rising expenses tied to technology and AI. A real risk is that higher structural costs meet softer capital markets or consumer credit, which would squeeze margins more than the bond activity suggests. The most relevant recent announcement here is the wave of fixed income offerings, including 6.40% Notes due 2056, 6.30% Notes due 2056 and multiple callable issues out to the 2040s. This cluster of long dated, unsecured, largely senior notes gives JPMorgan Chase flexibility in how it funds cards, payments, trading and private banking build outs. For you as a shareholder, the link back to catalysts is straightforward. A thick layer of term funding can support ongoing spending on deposits, payments tokenization work and wealth expansion without depending only on short term markets. The trade off is interest cost. If revenue growth or fee momentum softens while these coupons run, earnings and returns on equity could feel tighter than analyst models currently assume. JPMorgan Chase's current analyst narrative points to revenues of US$227.1b and earnings of US$68.8b by 2029, based on an assumed 6.8% yearly revenue growth rate and a move from earnings today of US$63.6b to that 2029 consensus level, an increase of about US$5.2b. Before this new wave of long dated JPMorgan Chase bond deals, the most cautious analysts were already working off 2029 earnings of about US$65.6b on revenue of roughly US$225.1b, with a lower 15.5x P/E. That is a much more pessimistic story on how rising funding and technology costs might reshape the narrative.
